newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE DELIGHTED WITH TREACHEROUS OPEN CONDITIONS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE DELIGHTED WITH TREACHEROUS OPEN CONDITIONS.

text.p: With the usual chorus of complaints about playing conditions at the U.S. Open rising all around him, Colin Montgomerie on Tuesday expressed delight with the treacherous layout the 156 golfers face.

"I'm anxious to get going. I'm looking forward to the challenge," the burly Briton said after just one look at the very demanding Congressional Country Course, where the Open is being played for only the second time.

With many players quaking in their spikes over Congressional's record length of 7,213 yards and par of only 70, Montgomerie, the leading player on the European tour for the past four years, was practically salivating as he talked about the daunting challenge.
"I love narrow fairways and long rough," declared Montgomerie, who has three top-10 finishes in the last five Opens, including a loss in a threeway playoff at very difficult Oakmont in 1994.
"All U.S. Open courses suit me," he added. "It is no secret that I drive the ball straight and, therefore, can hit from the fairway and give myself a chance for a birdie putt."

Montgomerie, who won the European Grand Prix last week after finishing fifth in the Volvo PGA Championship, said he relished the idea of playing a course that requires every possible type of shot -- but especially a long, accurate drive.
"This is as tough a golf course as you will find anywhere -- and that's as it should be," Montgomerie declared. "There is not one hole where you can relax."

With only two par 5s -- and neither really reachable in two shots -- Congressional is a collection of extremely long holes with tight fairways, punishing rough, 100 sand bunkers and four very dangerous water hazards.
"This to me is total golf," Montgomerie said. "The tee shot here really means a lot -- more than anywhere else in the world."

Montgomerie, whose father is Secretary of Royal Troon Golf Club in Scotland, where the British Open will be played in July, said his victory last week and his fine play in several prior weeks stood him well for the Open, which begins on Thursday.
"I'm confident with what I'm doing," he said. "But things can change Thursday morning.
"All I can do is try to bring my best game here. This course is such a demanding test it can break someone's confidence very quickly."
Montgomerie said the key was being prepared before the championship starts, which he feels he is.
"You have to bring your 'A game' with you," he admitted. "No one is going to find their game here this week.
"It is far too demanding a test."
